standfirst: A man who has failed at everything takes his own life and is sentenced to die twelve more times in twelve borrowed bodies. Eight fast hours, an absurd cast, and a moral argument you may want to throw something at. These six share the structure or the appetite for consequence.

picks.why: Death as a bureaucracy with a rescue mandate. Same afterlife framing and the same interest in the specific reasons somebody decides to stop. Both put a supernatural agency in charge of despair. Difference: Tomorrow is episodic and openly therapeutic, where Death's Game is a thriller that turns preachy at the end.

Debt, humiliation and a game with a rulebook. The same starting point of a man written off by every institution he touched, and the same use of a lethal structure to make him legible. Difference: it is an ensemble allegory about capital; Death's Game stays inside one man's head for eight hours.

A closed system that pays out for suffering. Same black-comic distance and the same escalation logic where the rules are simple and the people are not. Difference: nobody comes back, so its arithmetic is one-way and considerably nastier.

Twelve strangers, one afterlife corridor. Both use death as a switchboard: separate lives that turn out to be one story about who was left behind. Difference: the horror framing is a feint and the payload is grief, delivered quietly.

Dying treated as something you can still act on. Same idea that a wasted life can be redeemed in its final stretch, handled with far more patience. Difference: it is a hospice drama with no genre machinery, so the emotion is earned rather than engineered.

A man with a terminal clock and nothing to lose. Same fatalism and the same structure of a countdown forcing overdue conversations. Difference: it is a road trip romance, and the withheld conversation is the whole point.

against.title: Sweet Home
against.why: Paired for the platform and the genre swing. It is a monster siege with a fixed location and no metaphysics; the pleasure it offers has nothing to do with mortality.

against.title: Hellbound
against.why: Named because both stage divine judgement. Hellbound is about institutions and crowds reacting to the supernatural. Death's Game never leaves the perspective of the man being judged.

against.title: The Uncanny Counter
against.why: Recommended for the supernatural-agency premise. It is a warm ensemble action show about found family, and it will feel weightless straight after this.
